claims.text: The starting material is a homogenized, predominantly single-phase high-entropy alloy produced by conventional melting and rapid solidification or casting.
A controlled secondary annealing treatment can precipitate nanoscale coherent secondary phases uniformly throughout the matrix.
Secondary annealing that produces uniformly dispersed nanoscale coherent precipitates will improve strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance relative to conventional processing.
The effectiveness of annealing depends on optimizing temperature and duration to obtain a desirable precipitate size and volume fraction.
Overaging can cause precipitate coarsening and prevent the proposed property improvement.
Underaging can produce insufficient precipitation and prevent the proposed property improvement.
The treatment requires processing conditions that maintain precipitate coherence and prevent undesirable phase growth.
Uniform nanoscale coherent precipitates act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Precipitate–matrix interfaces provide sites for localized strain accommodation.
Impeded dislocation motion increases strength through precipitation hardening.
Coherent precipitate–matrix interfaces minimize stress concentrations.
Minimizing interfacial stress concentrations preserves ductility and fracture resistance.
A well-distributed nanoscale secondary phase increases Young’s modulus through improved load sharing.
The treated alloy will achieve more than a 20% increase in yield strength relative to the baseline single-phase alloy.
The treated alloy will achieve more than a 20% increase in fracture toughness relative to the baseline single-phase alloy.
The treated alloy will exhibit improved ductility relative to the baseline single-phase alloy.
The treated alloy will exhibit increased Young’s modulus relative to the baseline single-phase alloy.
Excessive or insufficient precipitation may worsen properties and negate simultaneous improvement in strength, ductility, modulus, and fracture resistance.
The optimal precipitate size, distribution, and volume fraction are uncertain because of compositional complexity and limited direct experimental precedent.

Failure of every tested annealing condition to produce a statistically significant simultaneous improvement, or observation of substantial property trade-offs at the optimum condition, would falsify the hypothesis.
